messages.author: 2430f2828c808219
messages.subject: slow sampling of a SEM
parts:
I having been trying Stan as an alternative to JAGS, where the structural equation models (SEMs) that I frequently fit can take 3 weeks to run!  This might sound like I'm doing something wrong, but colleagues of mine have similar run times (unless we're both do something blatantly wrong...).  Our datasets are not particularly large ('000s of observations), but the models seem to be intense computationally.

I have been trying to fit a Stan model to one of these SEMs, which only has about 200 observations (see attached, includes link to data).  It has taken a bit longer than a day to run 70,000 iterations, and I still haven't hit convergence.  I've gone over my code several times now and am a bit stuck as to where the efficiencies lie...  The painful centering step is included because I eventually want to standardize my parameters to a mean of 0 and sd of 1 to compare their relative effects.  But, the sd step is problematic (see https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/stan-users/cYjRmPY4k4E), so has been omitted for now.

Essentially, in this example, I have counts of three types of animals (denoted by y, y2, and y3) and I want to model their relative abundance, measured in different lakes and across years.  For one group, y, we want to model their abundance as a function of an unobserved latent variable called food availability.  This is affected by abundances of the other two groups of animals (y2 and y3), and is related to "phyto" densities.  Finally, we also want to model the effects of predation on y2 and y3, but many of the predator densities are unobserved, so we "impute" these given a separate regression.  I'm afraid that I can't provide a "simple" model for this particular problem - the slow sampling is very much context dependent.  Furthermore, many of the models I try to fit are complex and messy.  That is the reality of applying these methods in my field.  

So I guess my convoluted question is how can I make Stan run faster?  This is being asked a few times now, so perhaps worth a FAQ post...  But, I am trying to do the obvious here, i.e. vectorize and minimize operations within loops, and I have optimized my C++ compiler as per the RStan Getting Started guide.

Perhaps Stan can't / won't run faster for this particular class of problems?  I guess I was hoping that I would get 5-10X speed ups relative to JAGS (as found by others for their problems https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/stan-users/richard$20faster/stan-users/-_cVwdGgoqs/SKHN7yc8oCgJ).  Stan seems to get closer to convergence in fewer iterations than JAGS, but each iteration takes longer, especially when you can't run chains in parallel (which I do in JAGS).  For the record, I've been testing Stan on a pretty slow machine (2.2 Ghz).  I hope to get it running on my much faster 3.4 Ghz quad-core shortly.  Perhaps running it on there, with a chain on each core, and then merging the results afterwards, might be the best bet at this stage?  Again, would appreciate any thoughts on the topic.  I've just lived with the slowness of JAGS for too long and was hoping Stan would provide a great leap forward.  In fact, things are so slow to converge, I wonder whether we can even fit these models within the context of standard Bayesian packages...

Thanks again for your time. I realize that the questions are probably starting to get pretty repetitive at this stage, and more are arriving every day.  Hopefully the rest of us "users" can contribute more once we understand things better.

- Andrew

I have been trying to fit a Stan model to one of these SEMs, which only has about 200 observations (see attached, includes link to data).  It has taken a bit longer than a day to run 70,000 iterations, and I still haven't hit convergence.  I've gone over my code several times now and am a bit stuck as to where the efficiencies lie...  The painful centering step is included because I eventually want to standardize my parameters to a mean of 0 and sd of 1 to compare their relative effects.  But, the sd step is problematic (see https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/stan-users/cYjRmPY4k4E), so has been omitted for now.

Often it is possible to let Stan estimate undstandardized estimates and then you can later obtain standardized estimates with some R code or by specifying a generated quantities {} block in your .stan file. For example transformations, search for "standardized coefficient" in Long's textbook.

So I guess my convoluted question is how can I make Stan run faster?  This is being asked a few times now, so perhaps worth a FAQ post...  But, I am trying to do the obvious here, i.e. vectorize and minimize operations within loops, and I have optimized my C++ compiler as per the RStan Getting Started guide.

I just made a FAQ post at

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/J6ZItL2ZJ-IJ

In your case, you can vectorize these lines more

  for (j in 1:5) {                    // Priors on variance parameters
    for (k in 1:Nlakes) {
      varlake[k, j] ~ normal(intercept[j], sigmaLake[j]);
    }          
    sigmaLake[j] ~ uniform(0, 40);
    intercept[j] ~ normal(0, 1E3);
  }
  for (j in 1:4) {
    for (k in 1:Nyrs) {
      varyear[k, j] ~ normal(0, sigmaYear[j]);
    }
    sigmaYear[j] ~ uniform(0, 20);
  }

If varlake and varyear were defined as matrices, something like this should work

  for (j in 1:5) {                    // Priors on variance parameters
    col(varlake, j) ~ normal(intercept[j], sigmaLake[j]);
  }          
//  sigmaLake[j] ~ uniform(0, 40); // not necessary and slightly slower
  intercept ~ normal(0, 1E3); // vectorize

  for (j in 1:4) {
      col(varyear, j) ~ normal(0, sigmaYear[j]);
  }
//    sigmaYear[j] ~ uniform(0, 20); // not necessary and slightly slower

Remember that in Stan, unless otherwise specified, the prior is uniform over the (possibly limited) support of the parameter. So, explicitly specifying uniform priors does not alter the posterior and does entail some overhead. This won't make much difference with univariate uniform distributions, but for example, if you put a uniform prior on a covariance matrix with lkj_corr(1.0), then Stan wastes a lot of time.

Perhaps Stan can't / won't run faster for this particular class of problems?  I guess I was hoping that I would get 5-10X speed ups relative to JAGS (as found by others for their problems https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!searchin/stan-users/richard$20faster/stan-users/-_cVwdGgoqs/SKHN7yc8oCgJ).  Stan seems to get closer to convergence in fewer iterations than JAGS, but each iteration takes longer, especially when you can't run chains in parallel (which I do in JAGS).
 
 For the record, I've been testing Stan on a pretty slow machine (2.2 Ghz).  I hope to get it running on my much faster 3.4 Ghz quad-core shortly.  Perhaps running it on there, with a chain on each core, and then merging the results afterwards, might be the best bet at this stage?  Again, would appreciate any thoughts on the topic.  I've just lived with the slowness of JAGS for too long and was hoping Stan would provide a great leap forward.  In fact, things are so slow to converge, I wonder whether we can even fit these models within the context of standard Bayesian packages...

Parallel chains are somewhat possible now in rstan, along the lines you suggest. See

https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/3goteHAsJGs/discussion

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] slow sampling of a SEM

On Friday, October 12, 2012 12:34:14 PM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
Does the 'Matt' trick apply in all cases? I just applied it to my logistic regression model with limited capacity and things become worse, i.e. converting more covariates to the 'Matt' trick decreased the ESS horribly. So does the trick only apply for a certain class of models or does it apply in general and I should be worried about my model or whatever?

I would be worried about typos. Matt could probably come up with an example where it makes things worse, but in general it should be an option for any distribution in the location-scale family

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Location-scale_family

I think the Matt trick is primarily intended for parameters in multilevel models in order to reduce the correlations in the posterior distribution of the parameters. Doing it when data on are the left-hand side of the ~ probably shouldn't affect things much.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: slow sampling of a SEM
parts:
On Friday, October 12, 2012 10:03:34 AM UTC-4, atzap wrote:
I just made a FAQ post at

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/J6ZItL2ZJ-IJ

The FAQ post reads really well, and is very clear.  The one thing I'm not entirely clear about is the section on the shift-and-scale.  In your second box you have e_beta[j,k] and e_beta[j] expressed...  I'm confused by what the e_beta[j] syntax is capturing if e_beta is a j x k array...

This has confused many people. I personally prefer to define a two-dimensional thing as a matrix, in which case matrix[row,column] does what everyone expects. However, at the moment, Stan does not implement restrictions on the support of parameters in a matrix and sometimes you may want to use a multidimensional array.

But to answer your question

parameters {  
  vector[K] e_beta[J];         // errors in beta
}

This is "like" a JxK matrix, so this

transformed parameters {
  vector[K] beta[J];         // intercept + slopes
  for (k in 1:K)
    for (j in 1:J)
      beta[j,k] <- mu[k] + e_beta[j,k]*tau[k];
}

scale-and-shifts each element of e_beta to form beta. And this

model {
  for (j in 1:J) {
    e_beta[j] ~ normal(0, 1); // standard normal prior
  }

extracts the j-th "row" of e_beta and models it with a iid standard normal. However, in this formulation, it is not easy to extract the k-th column of e_beta if that were what you wanted. To do that, you would need to define e_beta as a matrix.

If you are very careful, you could alternatively define e_beta as a JK vector and avoid this loop, but then it is more tedious to map e_beta into beta in the transformed parameters {} block.

[Side note: In the next release of (r)stan, you will probably be able to do e_beta ~ normal(0,1); regardless of what e_beta is defined as]

Ben
